weeks.truth: In Christ you are not a project to be fixed. You are a new creation, reconciled to God by grace.
weeks.devotional: Most men carry a story about who they are: the screw-up, the provider, the one who has it together, the one who never will. Paul says something stronger is true of anyone in Christ. "The old has passed away; behold, the new has come." That is not a pep talk. It is a fact God declares because Jesus took our sin and gave us his righteousness (v. 21). This year is not about earning a new identity. It is about learning to live from the one you have been given.
weeks.pointman: Brothers, we start here on purpose. Before we talk about marriage, money or leadership, settle this: your worth was decided at the cross. Read like a son, not like an employee trying to keep his job.
reflect: What old labels do you still believe about yourself?
What does it mean that God made you "the righteousness of God" in Christ?
How would you live this week if you really believed you were new?
weeks.mission: Write down one old label you carry. Next to it, write what God says about you in 2 Corinthians 5:17-21. Keep it where you'll see it every morning.
discuss: Share one label you grew up carrying.
Why do men find it easier to perform than to receive grace?
What changes in a home when a man knows who he is in Christ?
weeks.endweek: Where did you catch yourself living from your old identity this week, and what did God remind you?
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that in Christ I am new. Tear down the old names I still answer to. Teach me to live as your son, reconciled and loved, not because of what I do but because of what Jesus has done. Amen.

memory.text: Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.

weeks.truth: Salvation is God's gift from start to finish. Good works are the fruit of grace, never the price of it.
weeks.devotional: Ephesians 2 opens with bad news: we were dead, not just struggling. Dead men don't help with their own rescue. "But God, being rich in mercy..." made us alive with Christ. Verse 8 is clear: by grace, through faith, and not from yourselves. Then verse 10 shows what grace produces: we are God's workmanship, created for good works he prepared in advance. Discipline without legalism starts right here. You don't read the Bible to get God to love you. You read it because he already does.
weeks.pointman: If you ever miss days this year, come back to this chapter. Grace is not permission to quit. It's the reason you can get back up without shame.
reflect: Where are you still trying to earn God's approval?
What does "you were dead" mean to you personally?
What good works might God have prepared for you this week?
weeks.mission: Thank God out loud, specifically, for three things grace has done for you. Then do one good work this week that no one will know about.
discuss: How would you explain grace to a coworker in one minute?
Why is it dangerous to think spiritual habits earn God's favor?
How does grace change the way we treat our families when they fail?
weeks.endweek: When did you feel the pull to earn God's love this week, and how did grace answer it?
weeks.prayer: God, I was dead, and you made me alive. Thank you for saving me by grace through faith. Guard me from pride and from shame. Let everything I do this year flow from gratitude, not fear. Amen.

memory.text: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.

weeks.truth: Following Jesus means daily handing him the controls, and finding real life on the other side.
weeks.devotional: Jesus never hid the cost. "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow me." A cross was not a burden you carried for a while. It was the end of your own plans. Daily matters too: surrender is not one big moment but ten thousand small ones. Yet Jesus attaches a promise: whoever loses his life for his sake will save it. Surrender isn't losing yourself. It's finally becoming the man God made.
weeks.pointman: Pick one area you've kept off-limits from God: your phone, your calendar, your money, your temper. That's where your cross is this week.
reflect: What area of your life are you most reluctant to surrender?
What does "daily" surrender look like at 6 a.m. on a Tuesday?
Where have you seen that losing your life for Jesus actually saves it?
weeks.mission: Each morning this week, pray one sentence before you look at your phone: "Lord, today is yours. Lead me."
discuss: What does surrender look like for a man who is used to being in charge?
What is the difference between surrender and passivity?
How have you seen a man's surrender bless his family?
weeks.endweek: What did you hand over to God this week, and what did you take back?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, I want to follow you, not just admire you. I give you my plans, my fears and my rights today. Help me pick up my cross daily and trust that life with you is better than life on my own terms. Amen.

memory.text: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

weeks.truth: Faith is confident trust in who God is and what he has promised, even when you can't see the outcome.
weeks.devotional: Hebrews 11 is a roll call of ordinary men who trusted an extraordinary God: Noah building in dry weather, Abraham leaving without a map, Moses choosing hardship over comfort. Faith wasn't the absence of questions. It was leaning their full weight on God's character. Proverbs 3 puts it simply: trust the LORD with all your heart and don't lean on your own understanding. Your understanding is real, but it is small. God's is not.
weeks.pointman: Faith grows like muscle: under load. Name the decision you're facing and bring it to God before you bring it to your spreadsheet.
reflect: Where are you leaning on your own understanding right now?
Which person in Hebrews 11 do you relate to most, and why?
What promise of God do you need to hold onto this week?
weeks.mission: Write down one situation you are worried about. Pray about it each day and resist trying to fix it yourself for one week. Note what happens.
discuss: Share a time God came through when you couldn't see the way.
How do faith and planning work together?
How can we model trust in God for our kids or the people around us?
weeks.endweek: How did God show himself trustworthy this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, I believe; help my unbelief. I bring you the things I can't control. Teach me to trust you with all my heart and acknowledge you in all my ways. Make my path straight. Amen.

memory.text: Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.

weeks.truth: Everyone has sinned, and everyone can be justified freely by God's grace through Jesus.
weeks.devotional: Romans 3 levels the field: "There is none righteous, no, not one." Not the worst man you know, and not the best. That honesty matters, because you can't receive a cure for a disease you deny. But Paul doesn't leave us there. Verses 21-26 are some of the best news ever written: righteousness from God, through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe, justified freely by his grace. Conviction is God's kindness. Condemnation is not his voice for those in Christ.
weeks.pointman: Men minimize sin or drown in it. Neither is the gospel. Call sin what God calls it, then run to the cross, not away from it.
reflect: Do you tend to minimize your sin or wallow in it?
What sin have you been calling by a softer name?
How does "justified freely" change the way you approach God after failing?
weeks.mission: Spend ten minutes this week in honest confession. Write it down, bring it to God, then destroy the paper as a reminder that it is forgiven.
discuss: Why do men find it hard to admit sin to each other?
What is the difference between conviction and condemnation?
How does a man's honesty about his sin affect his home?
weeks.endweek: Where did God convict you this week, and how did you respond?
weeks.prayer: Holy God, I have sinned against you. I don't want to hide or excuse it. Thank you that Jesus paid for it fully. Wash me, and give me a heart that hates sin and loves you more. Amen.

memory.text: for all have sinned, and fall short of the glory of God; being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus;

weeks.truth: God never tempts you, and he always provides a way out.
weeks.devotional: James traces how sin grows: desire, then conception, then sin, then death. Temptation rarely starts with the big moment. It starts with small permissions. Paul adds a promise: no temptation has seized you that is not common, and God is faithful. He will provide a way of escape so you can endure it. The way out is often early and unglamorous: closing the app, leaving the room, making the call, going to bed.
weeks.pointman: Know your patterns. Tired, alone, bored, stressed: most of us fall at the same times and places. Build your fences there.
reflect: When and where are you most vulnerable to temptation?
What small permissions usually come before you fall?
What "way of escape" has God already put in front of you?
weeks.mission: Identify your top temptation and put one practical guardrail in place this week. Tell one brother what it is.
weeks.alt: Identify your top temptation and put one practical guardrail in place this week. Tell one trusted brother what it is.
discuss: Why does temptation feel so personal when Scripture calls it common?
What guardrails have actually helped you?
How can we help each other without shaming one another?
weeks.endweek: Did your guardrail hold? What did you learn about yourself?
weeks.prayer: Father, lead me not into temptation and deliver me from evil. Show me the way out every time, and give me the humility to take it. Thank you that you are faithful even when I am weak. Amen.

memory.text: No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.

weeks.truth: God does not despise a broken and contrite heart. Real repentance leads to restoration and joy.
weeks.devotional: Psalm 51 is David's prayer after his sin with Bathsheba and Nathan's confrontation. He doesn't blame or bargain. "Against you, you only, have I sinned." He asks for more than forgiveness. He asks for a clean heart and a renewed spirit. Repentance isn't feeling bad for getting caught. It's turning around: agreeing with God, turning from sin, and turning toward him. And it ends in restored joy and a heart ready to help others return.
weeks.pointman: Repentance is a man's strongest move, not his weakest. The quickest way back to joy is honest confession.
reflect: Is there anything you need to bring into the light?
What is the difference between regret and repentance?
What would restored joy look like in your life?
weeks.mission: If you've wronged someone, go to them this week and own it without excuses. If there's no one, pray Psalm 51 slowly once a day.
discuss: What makes a real apology?
How did David's repentance differ from Saul's in 1 Samuel 15?
How do we create homes where confession is safe?
weeks.endweek: What did repentance look like for you this week?
weeks.prayer: Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love. Create in me a clean heart and renew a right spirit within me. Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Amen.

memory.text: Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.

weeks.truth: Obedience is love in action, empowered by the Holy Spirit, not a ladder to earn God's love.
weeks.devotional: Jesus ties love and obedience together: "If you love me, you will keep my commandments." Then he promises the Helper, the Spirit of truth, to live in us. Obedience isn't white-knuckled willpower; it's the Spirit producing a life that matches what we say we believe. Character is built in the small, repeated choices nobody applauds: keeping your word, finishing the job, being the same man at home as at church.
weeks.pointman: Character is what you are in the dark. This week, pick one area where your private life and public life don't match, and close the gap.
reflect: Where is God asking for obedience you've been delaying?
Where do your private and public lives not match?
How have you seen the Spirit change you over time?
weeks.mission: Do the thing you already know God has asked you to do but have been putting off.
discuss: Why is delayed obedience still disobedience?
What daily habits build character?
Who taught you what integrity looks like?
weeks.endweek: Where did you choose obedience this week when it cost you something?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, I love you, and I want my life to show it. Fill me with your Spirit. Make me the same man in private as I am in public, and help me obey quickly and gladly. Amen.

memory.text: If you love me, keep my commandments.

weeks.truth: Prayer is honest conversation with a Father who already knows what you need and loves to hear you.
weeks.devotional: Jesus assumes his followers pray: "When you pray," not "if." He warns against prayer as performance and gives a pattern instead. Praise: hallowed be your name. Submission: your kingdom come, your will be done. Provision: give us today our daily bread. Forgiveness: forgive us as we forgive. Protection: lead us not into temptation. You don't need impressive words. You need a closed door, an honest heart and a Father who is listening.
weeks.pointman: Most men don't pray because they don't know what to say. Use the Lord's Prayer as a frame and fill in your real life.
reflect: What keeps you from praying more?
Which line of the Lord's Prayer is hardest for you to pray honestly?
What would change if you prayed for your family every day by name?
weeks.mission: Pray through the Lord's Prayer line by line each day this week, adding your own words to each part.
discuss: How did you learn to pray, or did you?
What does it look like to pray with your wife or kids?
How can a crew pray for each other well?
weeks.endweek: What did you notice about God or yourself as you prayed this week?
weeks.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Teach me to pray. Make my prayers honest, my heart humble and my faith bold. Let your will be done in my home as it is in heaven. Amen.

memory.text: In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

weeks.truth: Scripture is God-breathed and enough to equip you for every good work.
weeks.devotional: "How can a young man keep his way pure? By guarding it according to your word." Psalm 119 isn't about information. It's about a man treasuring God's word like riches, meditating on it, delighting in it. Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture is God-breathed and useful for teaching, correcting and training in righteousness, so the man of God may be complete. You're not reading a textbook this year. You're hearing your Father speak.
weeks.pointman: Read with a pen. Underline what hits you. One verse you actually obey beats ten chapters you skim.
reflect: What helps you read the Bible with focus?
What verse has stuck with you so far this year?
Where do you need Scripture to correct or train you right now?
weeks.mission: Pick one verse from this week's readings, write it on a card, and read it at every meal.
discuss: Why is Scripture called "God-breathed"?
How do we keep Bible reading from becoming a checkbox?
How can we bring Scripture into normal family life?
weeks.endweek: Which passage spoke to you most this week, and what did you do about it?
weeks.prayer: Lord, your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path. Give me a hunger for it. Open my eyes to see wonderful things in your law, and help me obey what I read. Amen.

memory.text: Every Scripture is God-breathed and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness, that each person who belongs to God may be complete, thoroughly equipped for every good work.

weeks.truth: The Spirit grows self-control in us, training our desires to serve God rather than rule us.
weeks.devotional: Paul uses an athlete's language: "I discipline my body and keep it under control." Self-control is a fruit of the Spirit, not a personality trait for a lucky few. Jesus talks about fasting the same way he talks about prayer and giving: when you fast. Fasting reminds a man that his appetites don't run him. Saying no to something good for a short time makes room to say yes to God. This isn't about earning points. It's about freedom.
weeks.pointman: If you've never fasted, start small: one meal, replaced with prayer. The goal is hunger for God, not a diet.
reflect: Which appetite tends to control you most?
What would it look like to train rather than just try harder?
How could fasting draw you closer to God?
weeks.mission: Fast from one thing this week (a meal, social media, sports talk, sugar) and use that time to pray. If you have a medical condition, choose a non-food fast.
discuss: Where do men lack self-control most in our culture?
How do you keep fasting from becoming legalism?
What fruit of the Spirit do you want most?
weeks.endweek: What did your fast reveal about your heart?
weeks.prayer: Spirit of God, grow self-control in me. Free me from the appetites that rule me. Teach me to hunger for you more than anything else. Amen.

memory.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.

weeks.truth: God built us for rhythms of work, rest, private devotion and shared worship.
weeks.devotional: After a night of healing the crowds, Jesus got up very early and went to a desolate place to pray. If the Son of God needed time alone with his Father, so do we. Hebrews adds the other half: don't neglect meeting together. A disciplined life isn't a frantic one. It's built on rhythms: a daily time with God, a weekly Sabbath rest, and showing up with God's people. Men burn out when they skip the rhythm and try to run on adrenaline.
weeks.pointman: Look at your calendar. If rest and worship aren't on it, they won't happen. Put them on it this week.
reflect: What does your current rhythm of rest look like?
What keeps you from consistent worship with God's people?
When and where do you meet with God best?
weeks.mission: Plan one real Sabbath rest this week: a block of time with no work, no errands, and something that refreshes you in God.
discuss: Why do men resist rest?
What does a healthy weekly rhythm look like for your family?
How can we encourage each other to stay connected to church?
weeks.endweek: Did you rest this week? What helped or got in the way?
weeks.prayer: Lord of the Sabbath, teach me to rest in you. Slow my hurried heart. Give me rhythms that keep me close to you and connected to your people. Amen.

memory.text: “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth.”

weeks.truth: A husband is called to love his wife the way Christ loves the church: sacrificially, faithfully and for her good.
weeks.devotional: Paul's instruction to husbands is the highest bar imaginable: "Love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her." Christ's love moved toward his bride when she was unlovely, laid down his life, and works for her flourishing. Headship in Scripture is never about control. It's about responsibility and sacrifice. A man who loves like this goes first: first to apologize, first to serve, first to pray.
weeks.pointman: Single brothers, don't skip this week. Learn what Christlike love looks like now. It shapes every relationship you have.
reflect: How does Christ's love for the church challenge the way you love?
Where have you confused leadership with control?
What would "giving yourself up" look like this week?
weeks.mission: Ask your wife, "What is one way I can love you better this week?" Then do it without commentary.
weeks.alt: Ask a married couple you respect what sacrificial love looks like day to day, and serve someone in your life this week without being asked.
discuss: What does sacrificial love look like in ordinary life?
Why is "submit to one another" (v. 21) important context?
How can single men prepare to love well?
weeks.endweek: Where did you give yourself up for someone this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you loved your church and gave yourself up for her. Teach me to love like that. Make me the first to serve, the first to forgive and the first to pray. Amen.

memory.text: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it;

weeks.truth: Faithfulness begins in the heart and the eyes, long before it is tested in action.
weeks.devotional: Proverbs 5 is a father's warning and an invitation: "Drink water from your own cistern... rejoice in the wife of your youth." Faithfulness isn't only avoiding an affair; it's cultivating delight in the spouse God gave you. Jesus goes deeper: lust in the heart is already adultery. That's not meant to crush us; it's meant to show how seriously he takes our hearts and how much grace we need. Cut off what feeds lust, and pour into what feeds love.
weeks.pointman: Faithfulness is built with fences and fed with delight. Build the fence. Then go on a date.
reflect: What feeds lust in your life, and what would it mean to cut it off?
How can you grow in delight for your wife?
Who knows the truth about your struggles?
weeks.mission: Remove one source of temptation this week (an app, a show, a habit) and plan one evening of focused time with your wife.
weeks.alt: Remove one source of temptation this week and ask a trusted brother to check in with you about it.
discuss: Why does Jesus focus on the heart, not just behavior?
What practical boundaries protect faithfulness?
How can we talk about sexual integrity honestly and without shame?
weeks.endweek: What did you cut off this week, and what did you invest in?
weeks.prayer: Lord, guard my eyes and my heart. Make me faithful in private and in public. Help me delight in what you've given me and run from what would destroy it. Amen.

memory.text: Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the bed be undefiled; but God will judge the sexually immoral and adulterers.

weeks.truth: Godly communication is honest, gentle and quick to listen.
weeks.devotional: James gives a three-part rule men need daily: quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Paul adds that our words should build up and give grace to those who hear, and that we shouldn't let the sun go down on our anger. Most marriage fights aren't about the topic; they're about tone, timing and not feeling heard. A man who listens well is rare and powerful.
weeks.pointman: This week, practice listening until the other person feels understood before you respond. It's harder than it sounds.
reflect: Are you quicker to speak or to listen?
What tone do your family members hear from you most?
Is there a conversation you've been avoiding?
weeks.mission: Have one conversation this week where you only ask questions and listen, with no fixing or defending. Ask, "Did I understand you?"
discuss: What does "slow to anger" look like in practice?
How do you repair after harsh words?
What helps conversations stay honest and kind?
weeks.endweek: How did your words build up or tear down this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, set a guard over my mouth. Make me quick to listen and slow to anger. Let my words give grace to the people I love most. Amen.

memory.text: So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger; for the anger of man doesn’t produce the righteousness of God.

weeks.truth: Christ came to serve, and a husband shows strength by serving and honoring his wife.
weeks.devotional: Peter tells husbands to live with their wives in an understanding way, showing honor, as heirs together of the grace of life, "so that your prayers may not be hindered." Paul shows what that looks like: count others more significant than yourself, like Jesus who took the form of a servant. Serving isn't occasional grand gestures. It's noticing: what's heavy for her, what she needs, what would make her feel honored.
weeks.pointman: Learn your wife. What fills her up? What drains her? Serving starts with understanding.
reflect: How well do you understand what your wife carries day to day?
Where do you expect to be served instead of serving?
What would honor look like in your home this week?
weeks.mission: Take one recurring burden off your wife's plate this week and keep doing it.
weeks.alt: Take one recurring burden off someone in your life (a parent, roommate, neighbor) this week.
discuss: Why does Peter connect how we treat our wives to our prayers?
What are practical ways to show honor?
How did Jesus redefine greatness?
weeks.endweek: What did you learn about serving this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you took the form of a servant. Give me your humility. Help me understand and honor the people you've given me, and serve them gladly. Amen.

memory.text: You husbands, in the same way, live with your wives according to knowledge, giving honor to the woman, as to the weaker vessel, as also being joint heirs of the grace of life, that your prayers may not be hindered.

weeks.truth: God the Father runs toward his children with compassion, and earthly fathers are called to reflect him.
weeks.devotional: In the story of the prodigal son, the father sees his son "while he was still a long way off," feels compassion, runs, embraces and restores him. That's Jesus' picture of God. Psalm 103 says, "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him." Whatever your earthly father was or wasn't, your heavenly Father is like this. And fathers are called to show their kids a glimpse of him.
weeks.pointman: Your kids will form their first picture of God by watching you. That's not pressure; it's privilege. Run toward them.
reflect: How has your relationship with your father shaped how you see God?
Which son are you more like in the story?
How can you show your children compassion like the father did?
weeks.mission: Tell each of your children this week, "I love you, and I'm proud of you," and name one specific reason.
weeks.alt: Write a note of thanks to a man who was like a father to you, or encourage a young man who doesn't have a father around.
discuss: What did your father model well, and what do you want to do differently?
How does God's fatherhood heal father wounds?
What does running toward your kids look like?
weeks.endweek: When did you reflect the Father's heart this week?
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you for running to me when I was far away. Heal what my earthly father couldn't give. Make me a father, mentor and friend who points others to you. Amen.

memory.text: Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.

weeks.truth: Fathers are called to bring up children in the Lord's discipline and instruction without provoking them to anger.
weeks.devotional: Paul gives fathers a warning before an instruction: "Do not provoke your children to anger." Harshness, inconsistency, hypocrisy and absence all provoke. Then: "bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord." Discipline in Scripture is training, not just punishment. And training requires presence. You can't disciple kids you're never with, or never really with because your mind is on your phone.
weeks.pointman: Presence is spelled T-I-M-E. Put the phone in a drawer at dinner and look your kids in the eye.
reflect: How might you be provoking your children?
What does discipline as training look like in your home?
Where are you physically present but mentally absent?
weeks.mission: Spend 30 uninterrupted minutes with each child this week doing something they choose.
weeks.alt: Spend 30 uninterrupted minutes this week with someone younger who looks up to you (a nephew, a neighbor kid, a young coworker).
discuss: How do you discipline without anger?
What steals your attention from your family most?
What do your kids remember most about time with you?
weeks.endweek: When were you fully present this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me patient and present. Forgive me for the times I've been harsh or distracted. Help me train my children in your ways with a gentle, steady hand. Amen.

memory.text: You fathers, don’t provoke your children to wrath, but nurture them in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.

weeks.truth: Faith is passed down through everyday conversations, not just Sunday mornings.
weeks.devotional: The Shema calls Israel to love God with all their heart, soul and might, then shows how to pass it on: "You shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise." Faith transfers best in normal moments: the car ride, the dinner table, bedtime. You don't need to be a theologian. You need to be a man who loves God out loud.
weeks.pointman: Use Table Talk this week. One question at dinner. Let your kids see your faith is real, not a performance.
reflect: How often do your kids hear you talk about God outside church?
What normal moments could become teaching moments?
What do you most want your children to know about God?
weeks.mission: Pray with your kids at bedtime every night this week, and ask one faith question at dinner.
weeks.alt: Share something from your Bible reading with a friend, family member or coworker this week.
discuss: Who taught you about God, and how?
Why do everyday conversations matter more than lectures?
How can we teach the faith when we feel unqualified?
weeks.endweek: What conversation about God happened in your home this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, help me love you with all my heart, soul and strength, and let that love spill over to my children. Give me natural opportunities to talk about you every day. Amen.

memory.text: These words, which I command you today, shall be on your heart; and you shall teach them diligently to your children, and shall talk of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk by the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

weeks.truth: Each generation is called to tell the next about God's works, so their children set their hope in him.
weeks.devotional: Psalm 78 looks forward: "We will not hide them from their children, but tell to the coming generation the glorious deeds of the LORD... so that they should set their hope in God." The goal of legacy isn't a name or an inheritance. It's grandchildren and great-grandchildren who trust God. Some men are breaking a cycle; others are continuing one. Either way, faithfulness today shapes people you'll never meet.
weeks.pointman: Write down the stories of God's faithfulness in your life. Your grandkids will need them.
reflect: What spiritual legacy did you inherit?
What patterns do you want to end with you?
What stories of God's faithfulness should your family know?
weeks.mission: Write one story of how God came through for you and share it with your family or a younger believer.
discuss: What legacy do you want to leave?
How can a man break a generational sin pattern?
Why do stories matter so much in passing on faith?
weeks.endweek: What did you do this week that will matter in 50 years?
weeks.prayer: God of all generations, thank you for your faithfulness. Let my children and their children set their hope in you. Break what needs to be broken, and build what needs to be built. Amen.

memory.text: We will not hide them from their children, telling to the generation to come the praises of Yahweh, his strength, and his wondrous deeds that he has done.

weeks.truth: God owns everything; we manage what he entrusts to us and will give an account.
weeks.devotional: "The earth is the LORD's and the fullness thereof." That changes the question from "How much of my money do I give to God?" to "How do I manage God's money?" In the parable of the talents, the master entrusts different amounts to different servants. Faithfulness, not the amount, is what he commends. Stewardship covers money, time, skills, body, relationships and opportunities.
weeks.pointman: You're a manager, not an owner. That's freeing: it's not all on you, but it all matters.
reflect: What do you treat as "yours" that really belongs to God?
Which talents has God entrusted to you?
Where are you burying something out of fear?
weeks.mission: List what God has entrusted to you (money, time, skills, people). Choose one area to manage more faithfully this week.
discuss: How does ownership vs. stewardship change decisions?
Why was the third servant afraid?
What does faithful management look like at your stage of life?
weeks.endweek: Where were you a faithful steward this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, everything I have is yours. Make me a faithful steward of my money, time, gifts and relationships. Let me hear "well done" one day. Amen.

memory.text: The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.

weeks.truth: Godliness with contentment is great gain; the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
weeks.devotional: Paul doesn't say money is evil. He says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil, and that those who desire to be rich fall into temptation and a snare. The antidote is contentment: "if we have food and clothing, with these we will be content." To those who are rich, which by world standards includes most of us, he says be generous, ready to share, and set your hope on God, not on uncertain riches.
weeks.pointman: Debt, envy and overspending are spiritual issues before they're financial ones. Talk honestly about money with your wife and your crew.
reflect: Where do you see the love of money in your heart?
What would contentment look like this month?
Where is your financial hope really placed?
weeks.mission: Review your spending from last month. Identify one area driven by discontent and make a change. Talk about it with your wife or a trusted brother.
discuss: Why is money such a strong pull for men?
What is the link between contentment and generosity?
How do you talk about money in your home?
weeks.endweek: What did you learn about your heart and money this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, free me from the love of money. Teach me contentment. Let my hope rest in you, not in my bank account, and make me generous with what you've given. Amen.

memory.text: Be free from the love of money, content with such things as you have, for he has said, “I will in no way leave you, neither will I in any way forsake you.”

weeks.truth: God loves a cheerful giver and supplies everything we need to be generous.
weeks.devotional: Paul uses a farmer's image: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly. Giving isn't loss; it's planting. "Each one must give as he has decided in his heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver." Generosity flows from God's indescribable gift (v. 15). We give because he gave first. Generosity also includes time, hospitality and attention.
weeks.pointman: Generosity is a muscle. If you're not giving regularly, start with an amount that stretches you a little and grow from there.
reflect: Do you give reluctantly or cheerfully?
What would it look like to plant generously this year?
Who around you needs generosity right now?
weeks.mission: Give something this week that costs you something: money, time or a skill. Do it quietly.
discuss: What makes generosity hard?
How did someone's generosity impact you?
How can families practice generosity together?
weeks.endweek: How did generosity change your heart this week?
weeks.prayer: Thank you, God, for your indescribable gift. Make me a cheerful giver. Let my generosity point others to your goodness. Amen.

memory.text: Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.

weeks.truth: Your work matters to God; do it heartily, as for the Lord.
weeks.devotional: Before sin entered the world, God put Adam in the garden "to work it and keep it." Work is not a curse; it's part of our calling. Paul tells believers to work "heartily, as for the Lord and not for men," knowing that from the Lord we receive the inheritance. Whether you run a business, swing a hammer or manage a team, you can worship God through excellence, integrity and how you treat people.
weeks.pointman: Your job site is a mission field and a sanctuary. Do excellent work, tell the truth, and treat people like they're made in God's image.
reflect: Do you see your work as worship?
Where is your integrity tested at work?
How do you treat the people who work for or with you?
weeks.mission: Pray for your work and coworkers by name at the start of each workday this week. Do one task with extra excellence as an offering to God.
discuss: How does Genesis 2 change how we see work?
How do we keep work from becoming an idol?
What does integrity at work look like for you?
weeks.endweek: How did you honor God in your work this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, I give you my work. Let me do it heartily, honestly and for your glory. Make my workplace a place where people see Jesus. Amen.

memory.text: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord, and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

weeks.truth: Our struggle is spiritual, and God gives us his armor to stand firm.
weeks.devotional: Paul reminds us that we do not wrestle against flesh and blood. The battle behind your marriage tension, your temptation and your discouragement is spiritual. But he doesn't say "try harder." He says "be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might" and put on God's armor: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God, all held together by prayer. The armor is Christ himself.
weeks.pointman: Stop fighting your wife, your kids or your coworkers as if they're the enemy. Name the real enemy and put on the armor.
reflect: Where have you treated people as the enemy?
Which piece of armor do you neglect most?
How does prayer fit into spiritual warfare?
weeks.mission: Each morning this week, pray through the armor of God (Ephesians 6:14-18), applying each piece to your day.
discuss: How do Christians hold a biblical view of spiritual warfare without fear or superstition?
What does "standing firm" look like?
How can we stand together as brothers?
weeks.endweek: Where did you stand firm this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me strong in your strength. Clothe me with your armor. Help me see the real battle and fight it with truth, faith, your word and prayer. Amen.

memory.text: Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil.

weeks.truth: Courage comes from God's presence, not our own confidence.
weeks.devotional: Moses is dead. Joshua has to lead a nation into hostile territory. Three times God says, "Be strong and courageous." But notice the reason: "for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go." Courage isn't the absence of fear; it's obedience while afraid because God is present. And God ties courage to his word: meditate on it day and night. You're halfway through the year. This is a week to recommit.
weeks.pointman: Halfway. You've read about half the Bible. Don't coast now. Be strong and courageous.
reflect: What are you afraid of right now?
Where is God asking you to act with courage?
How has reading Scripture this year shaped your confidence in God?
weeks.mission: Do one thing this week that requires courage: a hard conversation, a step of faith or standing up for what's right.
discuss: What does biblical courage look like in daily life?
When have you seen a man act courageously?
How do we encourage courage without bravado?
weeks.endweek: Where did you choose courage over comfort?
weeks.prayer: Lord, you are with me wherever I go. Make me strong and courageous. Let your word fill my mind so that fear doesn't rule my choices. Amen.

memory.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”

weeks.truth: Jesus overcame temptation with Scripture, and he gives us his strength to resist.
weeks.devotional: Led by the Spirit into the wilderness, hungry and alone, Jesus was tempted three ways: comfort (turn stones to bread), spectacle (throw yourself down) and power (worship me and have it all). Each time he answered with Scripture. Hebrews says he was tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin, so he can sympathize with our weakness. James gives the pattern: submit to God, resist the devil, and he will flee.
weeks.pointman: Arm yourself with specific verses for your specific temptations. You fight better with a sword you know how to use.
reflect: Which of Jesus' three temptations do you face most?
What verse could you use against your main temptation?
How does knowing Jesus sympathizes with you change your approach?
weeks.mission: Choose a verse that speaks directly to your biggest temptation. Memorize it and say it out loud when you're tempted.
discuss: Why did Jesus use Scripture rather than argument?
What does "draw near to God" look like in a moment of temptation?
How can we help each other resist?
weeks.endweek: When did you resist temptation this week, and what helped?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you were tempted and did not sin. Help me resist with your word and your strength. When I fall, bring me back quickly to you. Amen.

memory.text: Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.

weeks.truth: We run with endurance by fixing our eyes on Jesus, the founder and perfecter of our faith.
weeks.devotional: Hebrews 12 pictures a race with a crowd of faithful witnesses who have gone before. Lay aside every weight and sin, and run with endurance, looking to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him. Hardship isn't proof God has left you. It's often his loving discipline, training you for righteousness. Galatians adds: don't grow weary in doing good, for in due season you will reap if you don't give up.
weeks.pointman: Missed some days? You're not disqualified. Get back on the track. Grace runs with you.
reflect: What weight is slowing you down?
Where do you feel tempted to give up?
How does looking to Jesus help you endure?
weeks.mission: Identify one area where you've grown weary in doing good. Take one small step back into it this week.
discuss: What helps you keep going when motivation fades?
How does God use hardship to train us?
How can we help a brother who is ready to quit?
weeks.endweek: What helped you persevere this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you endured the cross for the joy set before you. Help me run with endurance. Strip away what slows me down, and keep my eyes fixed on you. Amen.

memory.text: Let’s not be weary in doing good, for we will reap in due season, if we don’t give up.

weeks.truth: Jesus, though equal with God, humbled himself, and calls us to have the same mind.
weeks.devotional: Philippians 2 shows the greatest descent in history: Christ, in the form of God, emptied himself, took the form of a servant and became obedient to death on a cross. Humility isn't thinking less of yourself; it's thinking of yourself less and counting others more significant. Pride is the root of a lot of male sin: defensiveness, anger, refusing help, needing to be right. Humility is strength under God's control.
weeks.pointman: Humble men ask for help, admit when they're wrong and celebrate other men's wins. Practice all three this week.
reflect: Where does pride show up in your life most?
Who do you find it hard to count as more significant?
What would it look like to have the mind of Christ at home?
weeks.mission: Ask someone for help this week with something you'd normally handle alone, and publicly praise another man's work.
discuss: Why is pride so hard to see in ourselves?
How did Jesus model humility?
What is the difference between humility and low self-worth?
weeks.endweek: Where did God humble you this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you humbled yourself for me. Root out my pride. Give me your mind, so that I count others more significant than myself and serve gladly. Amen.

memory.text: doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself;

weeks.truth: We forgive because we have been forgiven an unpayable debt.
weeks.devotional: Peter asks how many times he has to forgive, and Jesus answers with a story about a servant forgiven an impossible debt who then chokes a fellow servant over a small one. The point lands hard: unforgiveness doesn't fit people who have been forgiven by God. Forgiveness doesn't mean pretending it didn't hurt, removing all consequences or immediately restoring trust. It means releasing the debt to God and refusing revenge.
weeks.pointman: Bitterness is a poison men drink for years. Name the person. Bring it to God. Start the process of forgiving.
reflect: Who do you need to forgive?
What do you think forgiveness requires, and what doesn't it require?
How big is the debt God forgave you?
weeks.mission: Write down the name of someone you need to forgive and pray for them every day this week. If appropriate, reach out.
discuss: Why is forgiveness so hard for men?
What is the difference between forgiveness and reconciliation?
How do we forgive when the other person isn't sorry?
weeks.endweek: Where are you in the process of forgiving?
weeks.prayer: Father, you forgave me a debt I could never pay. Help me forgive as I've been forgiven. Heal the wounds I've carried and free me from bitterness. Amen.

memory.text: bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, if any man has a complaint against any; even as Christ forgave you, so you also do.

weeks.truth: Loving your neighbor means stopping for the person in front of you.
weeks.devotional: A lawyer asks Jesus, "Who is my neighbor?" hoping to limit his responsibility. Jesus tells about a Samaritan, a despised outsider, who stops, bandages, carries and pays for a beaten stranger while religious leaders walk past. The question shifts from "Who deserves my help?" to "Who can I be a neighbor to?" Micah sums up what God requires: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your God.
weeks.pointman: Compassion is inconvenient by nature. Watch for the person God puts in your path this week, and stop.
reflect: Who are you tempted to walk past?
What keeps you from stopping for people in need?
How do justice and mercy work together?
weeks.mission: Help someone this week who can't repay you: a stranger, a widow, a struggling neighbor or a coworker in a hard season.
discuss: Who were the "Samaritans" of Jesus' day, and who are they today?
How can busy men practice compassion?
What does doing justice look like in your community?
weeks.endweek: Who did you stop for this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, give me eyes to see the people I usually pass by. Make me a neighbor who stops, helps and loves without counting the cost. Amen.

memory.text: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

weeks.truth: The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many.
weeks.devotional: On his last night, Jesus took off his outer garment, wrapped a towel around his waist and washed his disciples' feet, including Judas's. Then he said, "I have given you an example." In Mark 10, he flips the world's view of greatness: whoever would be great must be a servant. Real authority in God's kingdom kneels. Service is not a phase of discipleship; it's the shape of it.
weeks.pointman: Find the towel in your life: the thankless task, the job nobody wants. Pick it up this week.
reflect: Where do you expect to be served?
What is the "towel" job in your home, church or work?
How does Jesus' service of Judas challenge you?
weeks.mission: Volunteer for the least glamorous job you can find this week at home, church or work.
discuss: Why did Jesus wash Judas's feet too?
How does serving change a man's heart?
What does servant leadership look like in a family?
weeks.endweek: What towel did you pick up this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you washed feet and gave your life. Make me a servant like you. Let me find joy in serving, not in being served. Amen.

memory.text: For the Son of Man also came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

weeks.truth: God designed men to grow alongside brothers who sharpen, help and strengthen them.
weeks.devotional: "Iron sharpens iron, and one man sharpens another." Sharpening involves friction; real friendship isn't always comfortable. Ecclesiastes adds that two are better than one: if one falls, the other lifts him up, and a threefold cord is not quickly broken. Many men have plenty of acquaintances and no real friends. Isolation is dangerous. The enemy hunts the man who walks alone.
weeks.pointman: Who in your life can call you out and lift you up? If the answer is nobody, start a crew this week.
reflect: Who sharpens you right now?
What keeps you from deep friendships with other men?
Who could you reach out to this week?
weeks.mission: Invite one man to coffee or breakfast this week with the goal of going deeper than small talk.
discuss: Why do men struggle to build real friendships?
What makes a friendship sharpening rather than just fun?
How can this crew become a threefold cord?
weeks.endweek: Who sharpened you this week, and whom did you sharpen?
weeks.prayer: Lord, thank you for brothers. Give me friends who sharpen me, and make me a friend who strengthens others. Keep me from walking alone. Amen.

memory.text: Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend’s countenance.

weeks.truth: Confessing to one another and restoring each other gently brings healing.
weeks.devotional: Paul tells spiritual brothers to restore a man caught in sin "in a spirit of gentleness," watching themselves. James says, "Confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed." Accountability isn't a police force; it's a hospital. It works when there's trust, confidentiality and grace. And it requires going first: honesty is contagious.
weeks.pointman: In your crew, share one real struggle this week. Keep what you hear confidential. Respond with prayer, not lectures.
reflect: Who knows your real struggles?
What makes confession feel risky?
How can you restore a brother gently?
weeks.mission: Share one honest struggle with a trusted brother this week and ask him to pray for you.
discuss: What makes accountability healthy or harmful?
Why does James connect confession and healing?
How do we keep confidentiality in a crew?
weeks.endweek: What did honest accountability look like for you this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, give me courage to be honest and grace to receive others' honesty. Make our crew a place of healing, gentleness and trust. Amen.

memory.text: Confess your offenses to one another, and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The insistent prayer of a righteous person is powerfully effective.

weeks.truth: Christians are called to stir one another up to love and good works and to build each other up.
weeks.devotional: Hebrews says to "consider how to stir up one another to love and good works." Encouragement takes thought. It isn't generic flattery; it's noticing what God is doing in someone and naming it. Paul tells the Thessalonians to "encourage one another and build one another up, just as you are doing." Most men are starving for a word that says, "I see you, and God is at work in you."
weeks.pointman: Send three specific encouragements this week. Be precise: "I saw you do this, and it reminded me of Christ."
reflect: Who encouraged you in a way you still remember?
Who around you is discouraged?
What does God-centered encouragement sound like?
weeks.mission: Send three specific, written encouragements this week to men in your life.
discuss: What makes encouragement meaningful?
Why do men rarely encourage each other?
How can we build a culture of encouragement in our crew?
weeks.endweek: Whom did you encourage, and how did it land?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me an encourager. Open my eyes to see your work in my brothers, and give me words that build them up. Amen.

memory.text: Therefore exhort one another, and build each other up, even as you also do.

weeks.truth: Unity among believers shows the world that Jesus was sent by the Father.
weeks.devotional: On the night before the cross, Jesus prayed for us: "that they may all be one... so that the world may believe that you have sent me." Christian unity isn't uniformity. It's oneness in Christ that holds across personality, politics and preference. Psalm 133 says unity is good and pleasant, like oil running down Aaron's beard. Division is easy. Unity takes humility, forgiveness and a shared focus on Jesus.
weeks.pointman: Is there a brother you've drifted from or clashed with? Make the first move this week.
reflect: Where is there division in your relationships at church or home?
What does unity require from you?
How does unity witness to the world?
weeks.mission: Reach out to a believer you've had tension with and take a step toward peace.
discuss: What divides Christian men today?
How do we stay united when we disagree?
What makes a crew unified?
weeks.endweek: Where did you work for unity this week?
weeks.prayer: Father, answer Jesus' prayer in me. Make me a peacemaker. Unite us in Christ so that the world may believe. Amen.

memory.text: See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!

weeks.truth: God gives wisdom generously to those who ask in faith and seek it like treasure.
weeks.devotional: James makes a remarkable promise: "If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach." Proverbs says to seek wisdom like silver and hidden treasure; then you'll understand the fear of the LORD. Wisdom isn't just knowing facts. It's skill in living rightly before God. Leaders need it more than talent. The good news: it's available for the asking.
weeks.pointman: Before your next big decision, pray, open Scripture and ask a wise counselor. In that order.
reflect: What decision do you need wisdom for right now?
Where do you go first for advice?
What does "the fear of the LORD" mean to you?
weeks.mission: Bring one decision to God in prayer every day this week, and ask a wise believer for counsel.
discuss: How do you tell wisdom from cleverness?
Who are the wisest people you know, and why?
How does Scripture shape decisions?
weeks.endweek: How did God give you wisdom this week?
weeks.prayer: God, I lack wisdom, and I'm asking. Give it generously. Teach me to fear you, to seek understanding like treasure and to walk in your ways. Amen.

memory.text: But if any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God, who gives to all liberally and without reproach, and it will be given to him.

weeks.truth: The man of integrity walks securely; the one who takes crooked paths will be found out.
weeks.devotional: Psalm 15 asks who may dwell with God and answers with a portrait of integrity: walks blamelessly, speaks truth in his heart, doesn't slander, keeps his word even when it hurts. Proverbs adds that whoever walks in integrity walks securely. Integrity means being one thing all the way through. A leader's influence rests on it. It's built in small promises kept and lost in small compromises justified.
weeks.pointman: Keep your word this week even when it costs you. That's where integrity is forged.
reflect: Where are you tempted to cut corners?
Is there a promise you need to keep?
What does it mean to "speak truth in your heart"?
weeks.mission: Identify one area of compromise (time sheets, taxes, expenses, small lies) and make it right this week.
discuss: Why do small compromises matter?
How do you keep your word when circumstances change?
What does integrity look like in business?
weeks.endweek: Where did you keep your integrity when it cost something?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me a man of integrity. Help me speak truth, keep my word and walk blamelessly before you, in public and in private. Amen.

memory.text: He who walks blamelessly walks surely, but he who perverts his ways will be found out.

weeks.truth: In God's kingdom, leaders serve, shepherd willingly and lead by example.
weeks.devotional: James and John's mother asks for her sons to sit at Jesus' right and left. Jesus answers that rulers of the world lord it over people, "but it shall not be so among you." Peter, who once wanted greatness, later tells elders to shepherd the flock willingly, not for gain, not domineering, but as examples. Whether you lead a family, team, company or crew, you're a shepherd under the Chief Shepherd.
weeks.pointman: Three-quarters done. Lead by example: be the first to read, pray, serve and apologize.
reflect: Where do you lead, formally or informally?
Do you lead by example or by command?
What does shepherding look like in your role?
weeks.mission: Ask someone you lead, "How can I serve you better?" and act on the answer.
discuss: How is servant leadership different from weak leadership?
What leaders have you seen do this well?
How do you lead when you're tired?
weeks.endweek: How did you serve those you lead this week?
weeks.prayer: Chief Shepherd, make me a leader like you. Keep me from domineering or seeking my own gain. Help me shepherd willingly and lead by example. Amen.

memory.text: Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.

weeks.truth: Whoever is faithful in little will be faithful in much; to whom much is given, much is required.
weeks.devotional: Jesus describes a faithful manager who takes care of the household while the master is away and is rewarded with more responsibility. "Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required." In Luke 16 he adds that faithfulness in small things predicts faithfulness in big things. Responsibility isn't a burden to dodge; it's trust to honor. Men grow up when they take ownership instead of making excuses.
weeks.pointman: Own something you've been blaming on someone else. Responsibility is freedom.
reflect: Where do you make excuses instead of taking ownership?
What little things are you being faithful in?
What has God given you much of?
weeks.mission: Take full ownership of one problem this week that you've been blaming on circumstances or others.
discuss: Why do men drift toward passivity?
What does taking responsibility look like at home?
How does faithfulness in small things prepare us?
weeks.endweek: What did you take ownership of this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me faithful in little and in much. Forgive my excuses. Help me take responsibility for what you've entrusted to me. Amen.

memory.text: He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.

weeks.truth: The gospel is the good news that Christ died for our sins, was buried and was raised, and it is God's power for salvation.
weeks.devotional: Paul passes on what is "of first importance": Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, he was buried, he was raised on the third day, and he appeared to many witnesses. That's the core. In Romans he says he's not ashamed of it, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes. Before you can share the gospel, you need to be able to say it clearly and simply.
weeks.pointman: Practice saying the gospel in under two minutes. If you can't explain it, you can't share it.
reflect: How would you explain the gospel in two minutes?
Are you ever ashamed of the gospel? When?
Why is the resurrection essential?
weeks.mission: Write out the gospel in your own words in five sentences or fewer. Practice saying it out loud.
discuss: What are the essential parts of the gospel?
What do people misunderstand about it?
How has the gospel changed your life?
weeks.endweek: Did you get a chance to share the gospel this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you for dying for my sins and rising again. Make me unashamed of the gospel. Give me clear words and a bold heart. Amen.

memory.text: For I am not ashamed of the Good News of Christ, because it is the power of God for salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first, and also for the Greek.

weeks.truth: Always be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect.
weeks.devotional: Standing before King Agrippa, Paul tells his story: who he was, how he met Jesus and what changed. That's a testimony. Peter tells believers to always be prepared to give a reason for the hope that is in them, but to do it with gentleness and respect. Your story isn't the gospel itself, but it's powerful evidence of it. Every man in Christ has a story worth telling, even if it isn't dramatic.
weeks.pointman: Your testimony doesn't need a dramatic before. "God kept me" is a powerful story too.
reflect: What was your life like before Christ (or before you took faith seriously)?
How did you come to trust Jesus?
What has changed since?
weeks.mission: Write your testimony in three parts (before, meeting Jesus, after) and share it with your crew or family.
discuss: Why are personal stories so powerful?
How do you share without preaching at people?
What does "gentleness and respect" look like in practice?
weeks.endweek: Whom did you share your story with, or whom could you?
weeks.prayer: Lord, thank you for my story. Give me courage and gentleness to share it. Let my life and words point people to you. Amen.

memory.text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,

weeks.truth: Followers of Jesus are salt and light whose good works point people to the Father.
weeks.devotional: Jesus says, "You are the salt of the earth... You are the light of the world." Not "try to be." Salt preserves and flavors; light exposes and guides. Neither does any good hidden away. "Let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father." Your life is the first Bible many people will read. Integrity, kindness and joy make the gospel believable.
weeks.pointman: Ask yourself: if my coworkers only had my life to go on, what would they think of Jesus?
reflect: Where is your light hidden?
What would people around you say about how you live?
How do good works and words work together in witness?
weeks.mission: Do one visible good deed this week that points to God, and if asked why, tell them.
discuss: How can Christians be salt without being preachy?
When has someone's life drawn you toward God?
What dims our light?
weeks.endweek: Where did your light shine this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, make me salt and light. Let my good works point people to you, not to me. Let my life make the gospel attractive. Amen.

memory.text: Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

weeks.truth: Jesus has all authority and sends us to make disciples of all nations, promising to be with us always.
weeks.devotional: The risen Jesus gathers his disciples, some of whom still doubted, and gives the Great Commission: "Go therefore and make disciples of all nations." It's not a suggestion for professionals. It's a command for every follower. And it comes bookended by two promises: all authority belongs to him, and "I am with you always." Going might mean across the street, across the office or across the world.
weeks.pointman: Pray for three people by name who don't know Jesus. Ask God for one open door this week.
reflect: Who in your life doesn't know Jesus?
What keeps you from sharing your faith?
How do Jesus' promises give you confidence?
weeks.mission: Write down three names of people who don't know Jesus. Pray for them daily and look for one natural opportunity to talk about faith.
discuss: Why do you think some disciples still doubted?
What does making disciples involve beyond conversion?
How can we support missions as a crew?
weeks.endweek: What door did God open this week?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you have all authority, and you are with me always. Send me. Open doors for the gospel and give me courage to walk through them. Amen.

memory.text: Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.

weeks.truth: You are God's workmanship, created in Christ for good works he prepared beforehand.
weeks.devotional: We're back to where we started: saved by grace, not works. But Paul doesn't stop there. "We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand." The word for workmanship can mean masterpiece. Your purpose isn't something you invent. It's something God designed. Micah reminds us that it isn't complicated: do justice, love kindness, walk humbly with your God.
weeks.pointman: The last eight weeks are about legacy. Ask God what good works he has prepared for the rest of your life.
reflect: What has God shaped you for?
How have your gifts, experiences and even failures prepared you?
What good works might be waiting for you?
weeks.mission: Write a one-paragraph purpose statement for your life based on Ephesians 2:10 and Micah 6:8. Share it with your crew or wife.
discuss: How do you discover God's purpose for your life?
What's the difference between purpose and career?
How does grace free us to pursue purpose?
weeks.endweek: What did God show you about your purpose this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, I am your workmanship. Show me the good works you've prepared for me, and give me grace to walk in them with humility and joy. Amen.

memory.text: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

weeks.truth: The goal is not a strong start but a faithful finish.
weeks.devotional: Near the end of his life, in prison, Paul writes, "I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith." Many men start strong and fade: in marriage, in faith, in ministry. Paul finished. He also charges Timothy to preach the word, be ready in season and out, and endure suffering. Finishing well is built on daily faithfulness, not a final sprint.
weeks.pointman: Seven weeks left. Finish this race. Then keep running the longer one.
reflect: What would it mean for you to finish well in life?
Where are you tempted to coast?
Who is an example of someone who finished well?
weeks.mission: Write a short note to yourself describing the man you want to be at 80. List three habits that will get you there.
discuss: Why do some men fade in their faith?
What helps a man finish well?
How can we hold each other to the finish line?
weeks.endweek: Are you on track to finish well? What needs to change?
weeks.prayer: Lord, let me fight the good fight, finish the race and keep the faith. Guard me from fading. Give me endurance for every day ahead. Amen.

memory.text: I have fought the good fight. I have finished the course. I have kept the faith.

weeks.truth: Faithful men pass on what they have received to others who will teach others also.
weeks.devotional: Paul gives Timothy a four-generation vision: what you heard from me, entrust to faithful men who will be able to teach others also. That's Paul, Timothy, faithful men, others. Discipleship multiplies. Every man needs a Paul (someone ahead of him), a Barnabas (a brother beside him) and a Timothy (someone he's investing in). After this year, who will you walk with through the Word?
weeks.pointman: Ask God for one man you can invite to do FORGED52 with you next year. That's how this spreads.
reflect: Who has discipled you?
Who could you invest in?
What do you have to pass on that others need?
weeks.mission: Identify one man to invest in and invite him to read the Bible with you, or to start FORGED52.
discuss: What does discipleship look like day to day?
Why do so few men disciple others?
How could this crew multiply?
weeks.endweek: Whom did you invest in this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, thank you for the men who invested in me. Show me whom to invest in now. Make me faithful to pass on what I've received. Amen.

memory.text: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.

weeks.truth: Our light momentary afflictions are preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison.
weeks.devotional: Paul doesn't lose heart, even though his outer self is wasting away. Why? Because he's looking not at what is seen but at what is unseen. "The things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal." Eternity changes priorities. It makes suffering bearable, money less tempting and faithfulness worth it. We will all appear before Christ, and we live now in light of that day.
weeks.pointman: Look at your calendar and your bank statement. Do they show a man living for eternity?
reflect: How often do you think about eternity?
What would change if you lived with eternity in view?
What affliction is God using to prepare glory in you?
weeks.mission: Make one decision this week in light of eternity rather than convenience. Talk about heaven with your family.
discuss: How does eternity change how we handle suffering?
What does Scripture actually say about our future?
How do we keep an eternal perspective in a busy life?
weeks.endweek: Where did eternity shape a choice this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, lift my eyes to what is unseen and eternal. Let me not lose heart. Help me live today in light of the day I'll see you face to face. Amen.

memory.text: while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.

weeks.truth: God will make all things new and dwell with his people, wiping away every tear.
weeks.devotional: The Bible begins in a garden and ends in a city. John sees a new heaven and a new earth, and a loud voice says, "Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man." No more tears, death, mourning or pain. "Behold, I am making all things new." This is the end of the story you've been reading all year, and it's not just a hope for after you die. It's God's plan for all creation, and it shapes how we live now.
weeks.pointman: You've seen the whole story this year, from creation to new creation. Let that hope steady you.
reflect: What part of Revelation 21 gives you the most hope?
How does God's plan to make all things new affect the way you live now?
What tears are you longing for God to wipe away?
weeks.mission: Share the hope of Revelation 21 with someone who is grieving or discouraged this week.
discuss: How does the Bible's ending change how we read the whole story?
What does "new creation" mean for our work and lives now?
How do we hold hope and grief together?
weeks.endweek: How did future hope shape you this week?
weeks.prayer: Lord, thank you that you will make all things new. Come, Lord Jesus. Until then, let your hope fill me and spill over to others. Amen.

memory.text: He will wipe away every tear from their eyes. Death will be no more; neither will there be mourning, nor crying, nor pain, any more. The first things have passed away.”

weeks.truth: One generation commends God's works to another, and fathers bless their children in his name.
weeks.devotional: Psalm 145 says, "One generation shall commend your works to another, and shall declare your mighty acts." In Genesis 48, old Jacob lays his hands on his grandsons and blesses them in the name of the God who shepherded him all his life. A blessing is a spoken word of love, identity and hope. Many men never received one. You can give one.
weeks.pointman: Speak a blessing over your kids, grandkids or a young man in your life this week. Out loud, specific and rooted in God's promises.
reflect: Did anyone speak a blessing over you?
What do you want the next generation to know about God?
How can you commend God's works this week?
weeks.mission: Write and speak a blessing over each of your children or a younger person you mentor.
weeks.alt: Write and speak a blessing over a younger person you know: a nephew, a mentee, a young coworker.
discuss: What makes a blessing powerful?
How do we bless children when we have regrets?
What do you hope the next generation of men looks like?
weeks.endweek: Whom did you bless this week?
weeks.prayer: God who has shepherded me all my life, bless the generations after me. Let them know your mighty acts. Give me words of blessing to speak over them. Amen.

memory.text: One generation will commend your works to another, and will declare your mighty acts.

weeks.truth: Fruit comes from staying connected to Jesus; apart from him we can do nothing.
weeks.devotional: Jesus says, "I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing." This year was never about a reading plan. It was about abiding: staying connected to Jesus through his word, prayer and obedience. Branches don't strain to produce grapes; they stay connected. And Jesus says the result is joy, his joy, made full in us.
weeks.pointman: The plan ends next week. Abiding doesn't. Decide now what your daily rhythm will be after week 52.
reflect: What has helped you abide this year?
What tends to disconnect you from Jesus?
What will your daily time with God look like next year?
weeks.mission: Write down your plan for staying in the Word after this year: what, when and with whom.
discuss: What does abiding look like practically?
What fruit have you seen in your life this year?
How will this crew keep going?
weeks.endweek: How will you keep abiding after this year?
weeks.prayer: Jesus, you are the vine. Keep me connected to you. Let your words abide in me, and let your joy be full in me, this year and every year. Amen.

memory.text: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.

weeks.truth: God who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion, transforming you by renewing your mind.
weeks.devotional: You've read the whole Bible. Not because you're impressive, but because God was faithful. Paul urges believers, "by the mercies of God," to present their bodies as living sacrifices and be transformed by the renewing of their minds. And he writes with confidence that "he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ." You're not finished. You're forged, and still being formed.
weeks.pointman: Brothers, celebrate. Then call out the next man. The best way to finish this year is to start someone else's.
reflect: How has God changed you this year?
What passage or week will you remember most?
What good work is God still completing in you?
weeks.mission: Celebrate with your family or crew, share what God did this year, and invite one man to start FORGED52.
discuss: What did God teach you this year?
How have you seen each other change?
What's next for this crew?
weeks.endweek: What will you carry forward from this year?
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you for your faithfulness this year. You began a good work in me; carry it on to completion. Keep transforming me by your word, for the glory of Jesus. Amen.

memory.text: being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ.
